# Baylor Load Simulator: Vercel Deployment and Navigation

The Baylor Load Simulator app was deployed to Vercel production on 2026-04-14, fixing a server/client date-serialization bug along the way and adding persistent navigation between its `/reference` (Reference Card) and `/admin` (GPS Sync) pages. Active feature development continued into May 2026, including a Projected-vs-Actual comparison view and ongoing work to reconcile the app's data model with Catapult's real-world sync behavior.

## Key Points

- Neon (serverless Postgres) returns `practice_date` and `synced_at` columns as native JS `Date` objects rather than strings; these had to be serialized to ISO strings in the API routes before being passed to React client components.
- The Vercel project was not yet linked, so the MCP deploy tool could not deploy directly - `npx vercel link` had to be run interactively in a separate terminal first, as a one-time prerequisite.
- The `CATAPULT_TOKEN` value could not be pasted directly into chat (likely due to special characters); the workaround was to add it to `.env.local`, then have the assistant read the file and push the value to Vercel via the CLI.
- A persistent dark navigation bar was added to the authenticated layout, linking to the previously-unlinked `/reference` and `/admin` pages; it is hidden on `/login` and visible on all authenticated pages. A third top-level tab, `/comparison`, was planned on 2026-05-12 to surface the new Projected-vs-Actual comparison view (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]).
- `.vercel/` remains gitignored per standard practice (the project link itself is not committed), and `CLAUDE.md` was updated with the simulator's architecture, known gotchas, and deploy commands for future sessions.

## Details

The Neon date-serialization issue is a reusable lesson beyond this one app: any Next.js project querying Neon (or other Postgres providers using the `pg`/`@neondatabase/serverless` drivers) should expect timestamp/date columns to come back as JS `Date` objects, which are not directly serializable across the server-to-client component boundary. The fix - explicitly converting these fields to ISO strings inside API routes before they reach client components - resolved the deployment-blocking error.

Two pages, the Reference Card (`/reference`) and GPS Sync (`/admin`), existed in the codebase but had no way to reach them from the UI; adding the nav bar made them discoverable. The GPS Sync panel is functionally complete but not yet useful in practice - it will only become "live" once Catapult has actual GPS data for the practice dates being tested, which ties this deployment to the broader, ongoing challenge of getting reliable Catapult data into Baylor Athletics' various tools. Outstanding work includes connecting GitHub auto-deploy (Vercel dashboard, Settings > Git, with root directory set to `simulator`) so future pushes to `main` deploy automatically without a manual CLI step.

A month later, on 2026-05-12, development resumed with a `ComparisonChart` feature overlaying projected vs. actual practice load on `/practices/[id]/compare`, plus a confirmed plan to promote it to a top-level `/comparison` nav tab (see [[concepts/baylor-load-simulator-comparison-view]]). Building that chart surfaced a Catapult sync-aggregation issue - the same period type ("1 ON 1") appearing twice, non-adjacently, in a single practice's data - which the team chose to leave aggregated for now rather than redesign the sync model mid-season (see [[concepts/catapult-period-aggregation-sync-policy]]). This is the same recurring theme as the GPS Sync panel's dependency on Catapult data: the app's data model and Catapult's actual data don't always line up cleanly, and reconciling them is an ongoing, incremental process rather than a one-time fix.

# Custom Claude Code Skills: web-scraping, ingest-resource, improve-system

Three custom Claude Code skills - `/web-scraping`, `/ingest-resource`, and `/improve-system` - were built in a single session on 2026-06-10 using the standard "write-a-skill" process, and registered under `~\.claude\skills\`. The vault-facing skills were tailored to the user's actual SecondBrain vault structure rather than a generic structure inferred from prompt screenshots.

## Key Points

- `/web-scraping` routes by source type: free WebFetch first for static pages, Exa for semantic/discovery search, and Firecrawl v2 for JS-heavy/SPA pages; implemented as stdlib-only Python scripts (`exa_search.py`, `firecrawl_scrape.py`) that compile and fail cleanly when API keys are missing.
- `/ingest-resource` performs tiered acquisition (WebFetch, then falling back to web-scraping's Firecrawl script) and routes content by "shelf life": stable reference material goes to a new `Knowledge/` folder, active-work material goes to the existing `Projects/` folder, and `Notes/` (interview-me territory) and `Inbox/` are left untouched.
- `/improve-system` offers 5 modes - Audit, Skill Review, Experience, Historical Review, and Foundation - selected via signal-phrase routing; Audit mode archives rather than deletes and reports before touching anything, while Foundation mode hands off to `starter-voice-profile`, `starter-icp-positioning`, and `starter-design-tokens` skills.
- Both vault-facing skills were adapted to the real SecondBrain vault at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\`, including its existing frontmatter conventions and wikilink style.
- Verified API contracts: Exa uses `POST /search` with an `x-api-key` header; Firecrawl v2 uses `POST /v2/scrape` with Bearer auth. Real API keys still need to be added to `~\.claude\skills\web-scraping\.env` (currently commented placeholders).

## Details

The three skills were designed to compose with each other rather than operate in isolation: `/ingest-resource` calls `/web-scraping`'s Firecrawl script as a fallback when WebFetch alone can't retrieve a page, and `/improve-system` delegates to the `starter-*` skills for its Foundation mode rather than reimplementing that logic. This composition-first design means improvements to one skill (e.g., a new scraping technique added to `/web-scraping`) can propagate to the others automatically.

Newly written skills register immediately in the available-skills list as long as their frontmatter is valid - the user confirmed this by running `/reload-skills` and `/reload-plugins` after writing all three. The remaining open task is operational rather than design-related: the `.env` file for `/web-scraping` still contains commented placeholder keys for Exa and Firecrawl, and a live smoke test of both APIs was suggested once real keys are added.

   (e.g. "FLUSH_OK", or purely transient chatter). "An article already covers
   this topic" is NOT a reason to emit ===NOTHING=== - it is a reason to UPDATE
   that article with whatever this log adds.
3. Every article: complete YAML frontmatter (title, sources, created, updated)
   with `sources` citing 2026-09-16.md; at least 2 [[wikilinks]]; Key Points
   3-5 bullets; Details 2+ paragraphs; Related Concepts 2+ entries; encyclopedia
   style — neutral and comprehensive. Follow the AGENTS.md article format exactly.
4. Create a connection article when the log reveals a non-obvious relationship
   between 2+ concepts.
4b. Do NOT re-emit an article whose only change would be the `updated:` date or
   a restatement of what it already says. Measured on a real run, 4 of 5
   "updates" changed nothing but the timestamp - that is churn: it rewrites
   files, dirties backups, and invalidates caches while adding no knowledge.
   Re-emit an article only when you are adding substantive content.
5. Add one ===INDEX=== table row per article (new or updated).

Emit ONLY the delimiter blocks — no preamble, no commentary.

message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# DEV Sync 2026-09-22: Union-Merge Transcripts, Manifest Non-Discovery, and Cross-Machine Memory

A `/dev-sync` run on 2026-09-22 walked 146 repositories to bring the Mac in line with GitHub: two pulled (`_INBOX`, `DataBase_GPS_Reporting`), one pushed (`CommandCentre`), one cloned (`TOS_Evidence_Brief`, created on Windows 9/21), with 22 active and 117 dormant-and-clean, and no conflicts. Its durable findings concern how recurring cross-machine friction is resolved: a merge strategy for append-only logs, a manifest that does not discover its own new inputs, and the fact that Tier A memory does not travel between machines. Both findings recurred two days later on 2026-09-24.

## Key Points

- **Union merge is the right strategy for append-only transcript logs.** Mac/Windows conflicts in `global-memory/transcripts/*.md` resolve cleanly by keeping every line from both machines, producing no `.from-*` files to clean up afterward.
- **The manual form of the same resolution is to delete only the conflict markers.** On 2026-09-24 two clashing transcript logs (9/23 and 9/24) were resolved exactly this way — text from both sides kept, only the `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` lines removed — confirming that for this artifact class there is nothing to adjudicate whether the merge is automatic or by hand.
- **The backup manifest does not auto-discover new repos.** `TOS_Evidence_Brief` — created on Windows the previous day — was absent from `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`, which made the 09:05 backup report an error. Adding it fixed the report (backup of the prior file at `backup-manifest.json.bak-2026-09-22`). On 2026-09-24 the identical class reappeared as `manifest-unmanaged:RunningTheRoom`.
- **Tier A memory does not cross machines.** Durable GPS decisions were therefore written into the repo's own `docs/STATUS.md` *and* `global-memory/MEMORY.md` so the Windows machine would see them.
- **A folder name containing a space (`DEV/Linda Projects`) broke a sync step again** and had to be redone with the path quoted — a recurrence of the same hazard seen on 2026-09-11.
- **`compile.py` was deliberately not run.** A compile costs ~$1.28, so clearing the memory-compiler backlog was left as the user's call rather than taken as an auto-action; the warning persists in `.errors.log` until then, and had grown to 3 logs behind by 2026-09-24.

## Details

The union-merge finding names a resolution strategy that fits the artifact's semantics rather than a generic "take one side" rule. A transcript log is append-only and each machine appends independently, so the two versions are not competing revisions of the same content — they are disjoint additions to a shared record. Under that structure the correct merge keeps every line, and the usual conflict-file machinery (`.from-*` copies awaiting manual adjudication) is pure overhead because there is nothing to adjudicate. The 2026-09-24 recurrence is the same conclusion reached from the opposite end: presented with two logs already carrying conflict markers, the resolution was purely mechanical — strip the markers, keep both bodies — with no content decision required at any point. That a hand resolution and a configured merge driver converge on the identical output is the strongest available evidence that the strategy matches the artifact rather than the tooling. This is the same classify-by-kind-before-resolving discipline applied in [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]], where treating accumulating records as revisions would have discarded 324 unique forecast-log rows, and the same accumulate-versus-supersede distinction generalized in [[connections/newer-is-not-more-complete]]. Notably, the 9/22 PFF loader bug was the identical error one layer down — a replace where a merge was required.

The manifest gap is a recurrence rather than a novelty, and its recurrence is the point. A repo created on one machine does not announce itself to a backup manifest maintained on another; the manifest's coverage is declared, not discovered, so a new repo is invisible to it until a human adds a line. The 09:05 backup error was in this case an honest signal — the manifest check did fire — but the general hazard is the one catalogued in [[connections/silent-omission-defeats-per-stage-success]] and [[connections/aggregate-success-hides-a-shrunken-work-set]]: every managed item succeeds while the unmanaged item is never counted. Prior instances at [[concepts/backup-manifest-coverage-gap-2026-09-09]] and [[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]], plus the `manifest-unmanaged:RunningTheRoom` entry two days after this run, put the count well past the threshold at which — by the reasoning in [[connections/fix-the-generator-not-the-artifacts]] — the fix belongs in the discovery mechanism rather than in yet another manual manifest edit. Each individual fix is a one-line change, which is precisely why the structural fix keeps getting deferred.

The Tier A observation is a routing constraint with immediate practical force. Tier A memory is local to the machine that wrote it, so any decision that a second machine must honor — here, that the Mac owns the pulls and the Windows GPS writer is stopped — cannot live there alone. Writing it into the repository's `docs/STATUS.md` puts it in a location git already replicates, and mirroring it into `global-memory/MEMORY.md` reaches the synced memory surface; between them the decision arrives on the other machine by two independent paths. This extends the content-to-tier routing matrix in [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] with a cross-machine axis, and matches the working-machine-authors-the-fix pattern in [[concepts/fix-from-the-working-machine-handoff]]. Finally, the deliberate refusal to run `compile.py` is a recorded non-action rather than an oversight: a ~$1.28 spend is a user decision, so the backlog warning was left standing in `.errors.log` with the command documented in the compiler's README — consistent with treating `.errors.log` as an escalation channel that clears only on a verified clean run.

# Backup OOM-Killed During First-Time Indexing of a 547-File Memory Folder

An on-demand backup run on 2026-09-11 was killed mid-way by macOS for low memory during its memsearch INDEX step, which had stretched to roughly 20 minutes against a usual ~75 seconds. The cause was a newly-synced folder, `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs` (547 files, 6.4 MB — larger than the next three search folders combined), being indexed for the first time while a large chat session was concurrently resident. A retry was deliberately declined on the grounds that it would meet the same memory wall.

## Key Points

- **A first-time index is a categorically different workload from an incremental one.** The step's runtime went from ~75 s to ~20 min purely because a large new corpus had entered scope; nothing about the tool or the machine changed.
- **The index was left stale, not corrupt.** memsearch queries continued to work; the correct response was to defer the reindex to the scheduled 09:00 run on a quiet machine rather than retry immediately under the same memory pressure.
- **Two stale lock files would have blocked the next run** — one from the day's kill, one orphaned since August 5. Dead-PID locks are not self-healing and must be cleared explicitly; a kill leaves debris that silently poisons the following attempt.
- **Concurrency was the real trigger.** The index alone might have fit; the index plus an active large chat session did not. Memory pressure is a property of what else is running, which is why a quiet scheduled window is the right home for the work.
- **An explicit overclaim was recorded and corrected:** the backup had been called "working, will land shortly" while it was in fact heading for an OOM kill. CPU utilisation is not evidence of health for a long-running job.

## Details

This reproduces, on a Mac and at a different layer, the structural finding from 2026-07-27: hours-scale first-time embedding work cannot live in an interactive or session-attached context. That earlier diagnosis moved the heavy reindex out of the 45-second session-end hook and into the nightly scheduled backup task, on the reasoning that a session cannot absorb a job whose runtime exceeds the session. What 2026-09-11 adds is that *relocating* the work to the scheduled job does not by itself bound its resource footprint — the backup task inherited the hours-scale index and was killed by the OS rather than by a session boundary. The relevant ceiling moved from wall-clock to memory. The remedy chosen (defer to the 09:00 run on a quiet machine) addresses the concurrency half of the problem; the open question recorded for the user is whether `dev-docs` needs trimming or its own separate index, which would address the size half.

The stale-lock finding is the operationally sharpest item. A killed process does not run its cleanup path, so it leaves a lock naming a PID that no longer exists. Because the lock file is present and syntactically valid, the next run reads it as "another indexer is working" and declines — a failure that looks like politeness and reads, in a log, like nothing at all. That one of the two locks dated from August 5 shows the condition persists indefinitely and accumulates: a lock whose owner is dead will sit there through every subsequent run until something explicitly checks whether the PID is live. This is the same shape as the orphaned indexer processes left behind when in-session reindex tasks were killed twice on 2026-07-27 — a killed parent does not guarantee clean teardown of what it created, whether that is a child process or a file on disk.

The recorded overclaim deserves preserving as a discipline rather than an incident. Declaring a long-running job healthy because it is consuming CPU mistakes activity for progress; an OOM-bound process burns CPU right up to the moment the kernel kills it. The honest signals available were the step's runtime against its known baseline (~20 min vs ~75 s) and the machine's memory pressure, both of which pointed the other way. This joins a standing pattern in this stack of monitors that report on a narrower predicate than the question being asked — a dry-run that logged commits it never made, a `launchctl` exit code covering only scheduled runs — and the corrective is identical: name the predicate the signal actually covers before treating it as an answer.

# Mac-Owned GPS/Perch/VALD Pulls and Sleep-Induced Lateness

On 2026-09-21 the three Baylor athlete-data pulls — GPS (Catapult), Perch/PlayerProfiles, and VALD/ForcePlate — were moved off the Windows laptop and onto the Mac, and the same evening's closeout session verified the first afternoon of Mac-owned scheduled runs. All three exited 0 and carried data through 9/21, but two of the three finished roughly an hour late because the Mac was asleep at their scheduled time. The eventual decision, reached the following morning, was to accept the lateness rather than force a daily wake, on the grounds that the data arrived and only its arrival time was unreliable.

## Key Points

- **Schedule:** GPS 10:00 / 16:30, Perch 10:05 / 16:35, VALD 10:10 / 16:40 — all three now Mac-owned. The Windows scheduled task still fires at 8 PM but pulls nothing; see [[concepts/decommissioned-leg-verified-by-skipped-markers]].
- **Sleep, not the scripts, is the failure mode.** The Mac slept at 3:45 PM; GPS ran on time at 16:32, but Perch and VALD only crept forward during short background wakes and did not finish until ~17:36–17:39. Perch timed out twice before try 3 succeeded. This is the same root cause as the earlier 6:30 AM GPS problem.
- **Retries saved the run but do not make it reliable** — the correct framing is "late, not missing," and the revisit trigger was set accordingly: reconsider only if GPS data goes *missing*, not merely late.
- **The `pmset` wake was recommended on 9/21 and declined on 9/22.** The 9/21 closeout listed `sudo pmset repeat wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 16:28:00` as the recommended option and left it unset; the next morning Option 2 (leave sleep alone) was chosen instead. Both the enable command and its undo, `sudo pmset repeat cancel`, are recorded in `DataBase_GPS_Reporting/docs/STATUS.md`.
- **Windows VALD was already off.** The disabled step 1 in `refresh_all_data.bat` *is* the VALD step, and the Windows VALD pull had been broken since 8/2 — so the migration inherited a dead leg rather than duplicating a working one.
- **No alerts fired, so the Perch and VALD failure-alert paths remain unproven** — a successful-but-late run exercises neither the alert nor the absence of one.
- **Two writers would mean two mismatched databases**, so the Windows GPS writer was marked stopped (per Eric's report; not verifiable from the Mac), and the unused copy at `FA2026/_Mark_for_Deletion/gps_db_handoff_2026-09-21/` on Drive was queued for deletion.
- **The exposed VALD client secret was deliberately not rotated** — see [[concepts/deferred-credential-rotation-recorded-rationale]].

## Details

The substantive insight is that a scheduled job on a laptop has an execution precondition the scheduler does not enforce: the machine must be awake. macOS will grant short background wakes that let a long-running pull inch forward without ever giving it a contiguous window, which is why Perch timed out twice and both late jobs finished in a ragged ~17:36–17:39 cluster rather than at a clean retry boundary. From the outside, every observable signal is healthy — exit code 0, data current to 9/21, retries doing their job — and only the timestamp reveals that the schedule is not actually being honored. This is the same shape as the `Ready`-forever triggerless task in [[concepts/windows-backup-task-trigger-gotchas]] and the sleeping-laptop-misses-fixed-time-trigger gotcha recorded there: the scheduling layer reports truthfully about its own narrow predicate while the operational question (did this run when it was supposed to?) goes unanswered. The generalized version is catalogued in [[connections/the-execution-context-silently-edits-the-work-set]] — session lifetime, mount state, and now sleep state all shrink or delay what a run attempts without producing an error.

The `pmset` question is worth recording as a decision that was deliberated across two sessions rather than as a single call. The 9/21 closeout, written immediately after observing the hour-late finishes, listed the daily wake as the recommended fix; the 9/22 review declined it and attached a falsifiable revisit trigger instead. The reasoning for the reversal is that forcing a daily wake at 16:28 would make the afternoon pulls punctual at the cost of waking the machine every day for a job whose output is consumed the following morning anyway, so lateness inside a single day is not a defect in the consuming workflow. The condition that *would* justify the wake — data going missing rather than arriving late — is narrower and falsifiable, which keeps the deferral from decaying into an unexamined default. Storing the undo command alongside the enable command in the repo's own `STATUS.md` is the mechanism that makes the choice cheap to reverse regardless of which way it was decided.

Two ancillary findings deserve attention. First, the failure-alert paths for Perch and VALD have still never been exercised: a run that is late but ultimately successful produces no alert and therefore proves nothing about whether an alert would fire on a genuine failure. That leaves the alerting path in the same unverified state described in [[connections/alerting-path-must-not-share-the-monitored-systems-budget]] — untested alerting is indistinguishable from broken alerting. Second, the single-writer rule for the GPS database is a correctness constraint, not a tidiness preference: two machines writing the same database produce two divergent copies, and the Windows job being stopped is asserted rather than verified because the Mac has no way to inspect Windows' scheduler. The spare GPS database copy on Drive was queued for deletion for the same reason — a duplicate database is a future source of confusion about which one is authoritative. The cutover's durable record was fanned out to four repositories' `STATUS.md` files plus a handoff note at `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-09-21-mac-owns-data-pulls.md`, a placement pattern examined in [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]].

# Claude Memory Compiler Setup

On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` system — the same daily-log-to-knowledge-base architecture this very knowledge base runs on — was installed to give Claude Code persistent memory across sessions. The repo was cloned to `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`, Python dependencies installed via `uv sync`, and the knowledge base directory structure (`daily/`, `knowledge/concepts/`, etc.) initialized. This system is Tier C of a three-tier Claude Code memory architecture; see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] for the full picture including Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook scratchpad). On 2026-06-13, a day-long failure caused by `claude-agent-sdk` version skew revealed an important operational maintenance pattern.

## Key Points

- Three global hooks were wired into `~/.claude/settings.json`: `session-start.py` (SessionStart), `session-end.py` (SessionEnd), and `pre-compact.py` (PreCompact).
- Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.
- All script invocations follow the `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler <script>` pattern, guaranteeing the correct virtualenv context regardless of the current working directory when a hook fires.
- Hook configuration changes are not picked up live — they require a full Claude Code restart (or a `/hooks` reload) before they take effect.
- After 6 PM local time, the `flush.py` background process automatically triggers `compile.py` to turn that day's daily log into knowledge articles, without manual intervention. Manual queries are also available via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/query.py "<question>"`.
- **The agent itself never receives a "session ending" notification** — SessionEnd and PreCompact are harness-level events; the harness runs the hook shell commands, not the agent. Teardown logic must live in the hook, not in agent-side instructions.
- **Version skew failure mode:** the memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk` to a specific version, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary. When the system Claude Code auto-updates (e.g., from 2.1.92 to 2.1.177), the bundled CLI in the venv falls behind and eventually cannot parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json`, causing every `flush.py` invocation to exit immediately with a non-zero code. Symptom: 100% FLUSH_ERROR rate after a Claude Code update, despite no changes to the memory compiler itself.
- **Fix for version skew:** `cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`. This upgrades only the `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and its bundled CLI to match the current system version without touching other pinned dependencies. Run this whenever FLUSH_ERRORs appear after a Claude Code auto-update.
- **Diagnostic caution:** do NOT invoke the bundled `claude.exe` CLI directly to diagnose version skew — it spawns a real nested agent session. Instead, inspect venv package metadata (e.g., `uv pip show claude-agent-sdk`) to check the installed version against the system CLI version.

## Details

The setup session focused on making the memory pipeline reliable rather than merely functional. The PATH issue with `uv` is a generalizable lesson for any Claude Code hook that shells out to a tool installed via `uv`, `pipx`, or similar user-local installers: hook processes may run with a minimal environment, so absolute paths (or explicit `PATH` exports) are safer than relying on the interactive shell's configuration. Similarly, the `uv run --directory` pattern avoids a whole class of "wrong virtualenv" bugs that would otherwise occur if a hook fires while Claude Code's working directory is some unrelated project.

Once restarted, the three hooks form a closed loop: `session-start.py` injects the current knowledge index and the most recent daily log into every new session's context (capped at 20,000 characters), `session-end.py` and `pre-compact.py` capture the raw conversation transcript and spawn a detached `flush.py` process, and `flush.py` decides what's worth appending to the day's daily log and, after 6 PM, kicks off `compile.py` to synthesize that log into structured `knowledge/` articles. PreCompact serves as a safety net for long sessions: in a session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, ensuring at least one compiled log exists even if the session later crashes before SessionEnd fires.

The 2026-06-13 version skew failure is operationally important. On that day, Claude Code auto-updated from approximately version 2.1.92 to 2.1.177 — 85 releases ahead — while the memory compiler's venv still bundled the older CLI via `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56`. The newer `~/.claude/settings.json` included hooks, settings, or schemas added after version 2.1.92 that the stale bundled CLI could not parse; every `flush.py` call exited on startup without processing the session. The failure was isolated entirely to the Tier C compile layer: Tier B (the `transcript-capture.js` Stop-hook) continued capturing sessions uninterrupted because it has no dependency on `claude-agent-sdk`. Twenty-four days of continuous Tier B logs and four sessions captured on the failure day itself confirmed the architectural independence. This means that during a version-skew failure, raw session context is preserved in Tier B transcripts and can be backfilled after the fix is applied. The `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync` fix is surgical — it upgrades only the affected package without touching other pinned dependencies — and is safe to apply at any time. A post-fix test flush verifies the fix before trusting that normal operation has resumed. See [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] for the architectural insight this failure demonstrated empirically.

- [[concepts/claude-code-environment-maintenance]] — A later (2026-06-10) maintenance pass on the same Claude Code environment, addressing plugin/MCP configuration drift in the broader tooling this memory system runs inside.
- [[concepts/daily-onramp-automation]] — Another automation pipeline (built 2026-06-10) sharing the same token-efficiency motivation: pre-process inputs so the LLM only has to read a compact summary.

# Closing a 49-Folder Backup Manifest Coverage Gap

On 2026-09-09 a KeystoneOS daily backup run returned `status: ERROR` with two problems: the `~/.claude` repo was one commit behind GitHub (blocking its push) and 49 folders under `~/DEV` were absent from `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json`. Rather than triage the 49, the user confirmed that all of them mattered — the gap was a residue of an earlier migration — and every one was added. The manifest grew from 78 to 125 entries and the backup's job count went from 28 to 76.

## Key Points

- **The gap was invisible.** Folders absent from the manifest are never backed up, and their absence produces no error that reads as urgent — only an advisory `manifest-unmanaged` class. The 49-folder hole had existed since a prior migration.
- **All 49 were added, not triaged:** 47 as git repos (working-tree capture to the CRASHBOX SSD) and 2 as plain folders (`_ARCHIVE`, `docs` — SSD copy only, no repo semantics).
- **Two stale entries were removed** (`AI_Analyst`, `token-dashboard`) after confirming both had already moved into `~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/`, leaving 125 entries. Manifest hygiene runs in both directions: adding new folders and retiring moved ones.
- **`DexaProject`'s warning was kept deliberately** — it lives on Google Drive intentionally, so its manifest complaint is an accepted permanent condition rather than a defect to silence. A separate later finding in the same day established that the *GitHub* copy of `DexaProject` still holds a patient CSV and must be deleted.
- **The `~/.claude` behind-by-one state was resolved with `git pull --rebase --autostash`,** preserving two uncommitted edits (`settings.json`, `hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh`). Backups never auto-merge by design.
- **Commits were made but not pushed** — `~/.claude` at `dc54c97` and `~/.claude/global-memory` at `38e462b` — with the push deliberately left to the next scheduled backup run.

## Details

This is the largest instance yet of the manifest-drift failure class first catalogued in [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]] (three folders) and re-observed at [[concepts/backup-error-log-recurring-failures-2026-08-16]] (five folders). The escalation from three to five to forty-nine is informative: the earlier gaps were ordinary drift from folders created faster than manifest entries, whereas this one had a single structural cause — a migration that moved or created many directories at once while the manifest, being hand-maintained, stayed where it was. Bulk moves are precisely the event a curated list cannot survive, which strengthens the standing proposal in [[concepts/dev-folder-manifest-default-deny]] to derive the manifest from a directory scan rather than maintaining it by hand. The default-deny guard did its job in that the folders were reported rather than silently excluded, but reporting alone is only sufficient when the report is acted on, and forty-nine entries accumulating across weeks shows the report being observed and deferred.

The removal of `AI_Analyst` and `token-dashboard` is the neglected half of manifest maintenance. A manifest entry pointing at a folder that has moved into `_ARCHIVE` will either fail loudly (noise) or resolve to a stale path (worse), and neither outcome is caught by any check that only asks "is every folder covered?" The `DexaProject` decision demonstrates the third state a manifest entry can occupy: an accepted, documented exception whose warning is expected output rather than a pending task. Recording the reason — it lives on Google Drive intentionally — is what prevents a future maintenance pass from either "fixing" it or being confused by it, the same discipline applied to the two large graph files kept deliberately in the 2026-09-01 classification pass. Notably, the same day's repo-visibility audit found that this deliberate local exception coexists with a genuine problem at a different layer: `erash11/DexaProject` is still a GitHub repository containing a patient CSV, awaiting deletion. A documented exception on one axis does not clear the artifact on every axis.

The `git pull --rebase --autostash` choice is worth isolating as policy. The backup job pushes several repos, and a repo that is behind its remote cannot push; the tempting resolutions are a force-push (destroys remote history) or a merge (creates a commit the operator did not author). Rebasing with autostash preserves both the remote's history and the two uncommitted working-tree edits, and the stated principle — backups never auto-merge — keeps the backup system from making content decisions on the operator's behalf. This is the same restraint shown when a two-writer SecondBrain conflict was resolved by staging both sides rather than adjudicating it, per [[concepts/stack-doctor-sweep-2026-08-11]]. The decision to commit `~/.claude` and `global-memory` without pushing follows the same logic in the other direction: the push is the backup's job, so leaving it to the next scheduled run keeps one owner for that action rather than racing it.

# Stack Doctor Sweep (2026-08-11): Self-Inflicted Repo Divergence and a Lying Dry Run

A `/claude-stack-doctor` run on 2026-08-11 after a three-day gap took the automation/memory stack from 8 issues to 6 (three of the remaining six being lagging indicators that clear on the next nightly backup). The sweep's most valuable findings were not the fixes themselves but three cases where the *monitoring layer* was the defect: a nightly backup that committed its own generated files and so diverged a repo every night, a `skill-tax` check measuring the wrong quantity, and a `-DryRun` flag that reported git operations it never performed.

## Key Points

- **`repo-diverged:skills` was self-inflicted.** Six tracked files were regenerated every run (`last-weekly-run.log` plus five `__pycache__` entries), so the nightly backup committed churn and diverged the repo nightly. Untracking and gitignoring them was the sweep's highest-leverage fix.
- **`daily-backup.ps1 -DryRun` was lying.** The `Log` calls at lines 28/38 sat *outside* the `if (-not $DryRun)` guards at 24/34, so a dry run printed "committed / pushed" for git operations it never ran — briefly fooling the sweep itself. Fixed to `[dry-run] would commit`.
- **`skill-tax` was a false positive from the monitor's own logic:** it counted all 133 on-disk `SKILL.md` files with no knowledge of `skillOverrides`. Verified empirically first (0 of 72 overridden skills leak into the listing; 61 expected, 60 seen), *then* the script was patched — the two candidate fixes were opposite, so the discriminating check had to precede either.
- **`flush-error` recurrence across 8/08 and 8/11 indicated version skew, not contention:** `claude-agent-sdk` was 26 versions behind (0.2.110 → 0.2.136); upgrading restored flushes, and the memsearch flush patch was confirmed to survive the package operation.
- **Both sides preserved on a two-writer conflict.** Four SecondBrain morning briefings differed from committed origin versions; origin's won by default and are live, with local copies staged at `doctor-backup-20260807-135924/secondbrain-local-briefings/*.local.md` — fully reversible rather than adjudicated on the spot.

## Details

The three monitoring-layer defects share a structure worth naming: each produced a confident, well-formatted signal about a system state it was not actually measuring. The dry-run bug is the purest form — logging placed outside the guard it describes means the flag's entire purpose (previewing without acting) is silently void, and the operator's trust in the preview is inversely related to its accuracy. `skill-tax` is the same failure one level up: the check counted files on disk, a proxy that was correct before `skillOverrides` existed and became wrong afterward, so a previously-completed cleanup appeared not to have landed. The correct response in that case was explicitly *not* to fix either candidate immediately, because the two possible remedies (clean up more skills, or patch the counter) pointed in opposite directions; running the discriminating check first — do overridden skills leak into the listing? — decided which. The `repo-diverged:skills` case is the automation eating its own output: a backup job that commits generated artifacts guarantees divergence on every run, making a real alarm fire nightly for a cause the alarm cannot describe.

The sweep's restraint is as instructive as its fixes. Several issues were deliberately left alone with reasons recorded: 73 unversioned skill files (a design fork — adding `~/.agents/skills` to `backup-manifest.json` was proposed but not applied), unmanaged `DEV` directories (the user's scope call), a 4-log compiler backlog (self-healing at 2/night against ~1/day, and forcing it costs real money), and `snapshot:sessions` (an rsync race against a live Codex file, not rot). Two items were escalated as genuinely not auto-fixable and left open: Outlook auth expired, so morning briefings were shipping with 0 email threads pending an interactive `reauth.sh` run, and Google Drive 154h stale, with files reaching the local `G:` cache but GoogleDriveFS not syncing. The `MEMORY.md` file was at 100% — the next write would have failed — and was consolidated to 93% by shortening wording while keeping all 16 threads, rather than dropping any. Finally, two `flush-error` session IDs were classified benign only after evidence (the IDs exist nowhere; the DEV slug holds 28 transcripts, 3 in the last 24h), on the explicit principle of not classifying by inference; and two self-corrections were made before reporting (an "8 → 2" claim against a raw verdict of 6, and a claim that the /doctor changes were unversioned when the nightly backup had in fact committed them).

# Tier A Memory, Not a Handoff Doc, as the Output of a Verification Session

At the 2026-09-07 closeout of a Baylor tech-inventory verification session, the durable output was deliberately written as a Tier A project memory file (`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/project_tech-inventory-refresh.md`) rather than as a handoff document. The stated reason was that the session had been a verification check rather than a build: it produced no artifacts, changed no code, and left no in-progress state to resume — its entire durable payload was one trap and one command, which is memory-shaped rather than handoff-shaped.

## Key Points

- **The routing rule is what the session produced, not how long it ran.** A build leaves partial state, open decisions, and a resumption point — handoff material. A verification check leaves a finding and possibly a command — memory material.
- **The payload was exactly two things:** the Microsoft-Forms-vs-Google-Forms platform trap, and the refresh command to run once a new export lands. Both are facts a future session needs loaded, not narrative a future session needs to read.
- **An index line was added to the slug's `MEMORY.md`** alongside the new file, keeping the pointer layer consistent with the content layer rather than leaving an unindexed orphan.
- **The same session trimmed `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` from 2,531 → 2,496 characters** by removing four lines whose detail now lives in Tier A — the third over-cap fix of the day, again by relocation with no fact lost.
- **Nothing was committed, for a structural reason rather than a deferral:** KeystoneOS was clean and `Tech_Inventory_Analysis` is not a git repository at all, so the finding's only durable home *is* the memory tier.

## Details

The handoff-versus-memory distinction is worth stating as policy because the two have different readers and different lifetimes. A handoff document is addressed to the next session on the same task and is written to be read once, then discarded when the task closes; it carries narrative, sequencing, and "where I stopped." A Tier A memory file is addressed to every future session in that project slug and is written to be loaded silently and indefinitely; it carries invariants. Writing this session's output as a handoff would have buried a permanent trap — that the documented form IDs are the wrong platform — inside a document whose relevance nominally expires when the inventory project ships. Writing it as memory guarantees the trap is present the next time anyone touches the project, which is precisely when the `gws` false-negative would otherwise be walked into. The same reasoning applies in reverse in [[concepts/handoff-document-placement-discipline]] and [[concepts/handoff-doc-uncommitted-tooling-changes]], where genuinely in-progress build state needed a document rather than a memory line.

The non-git detail sharpens the argument. Because `Tech_Inventory_Analysis` is not under version control, there is no repository in which a `NOTES.md` or `docs/` addition would be preserved, reviewed, or backed up through the git leg of the backup pipeline. The memory tier is therefore not merely the tidier home for this finding but the only one that is both durable and automatically captured — the `~/.claude` repo is backed up on the 09:00 job, whereas an untracked file inside a non-repo project folder depends on manifest coverage, which is exactly the coverage that has drifted before per [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]]. Recording a fact in a location the backup system can see is part of making it durable, not a separate concern.

Two operational details recurred from earlier in the same day. The global `MEMORY.md` was again over its 2,500-character cap and was again relieved by relocating detail into Tier A rather than deleting it — the third instance on 2026-09-07, reinforcing that the file's normal working volume sits at the cap and that migration is the only remedy with staying power. And a shell guard again blocked a redirect writing into the home directory, forcing a fall back to the Write tool; this was explicitly logged as the second occurrence that day, which promotes it from an incident to a known route: memory files are written with the native file tools, not shell redirection.

# Claude Code Worktree Gotchas: Branch Orphan, CRLF Normalization, and Windows MAX_PATH

Three non-obvious gotchas around Claude Code's worktree workflow have been documented across sessions. On 2026-05-22, `ExitWorktree` with the `remove` flag deletes the associated branch along with the worktree directory (orphaning any unmerged commits), and Windows `autocrlf` normalization can make files appear different in the working tree even when they are byte-identical inside the Git object store. On 2026-06-17, a third class of failure emerged: Windows MAX_PATH limits on deeply-nested long-filename directories (e.g., PDF libraries in `SourcePapers/`) silently break `git worktree add` / `EnterWorktree`, requiring a sparse-checkout workaround or outright disabling of background-isolation enforcement in `.claude/settings.json`. Additionally, CRLF phantom diffs that accumulate after branch operations can be cleared with `git update-index --refresh` without touching working-tree file content.

## Key Points

- **`ExitWorktree remove` deletes the branch:** the `remove` option on `ExitWorktree` removes both the worktree filesystem and its associated branch in a single operation. Any commits made on that branch that have not been merged or cherry-picked are orphaned — they still exist in the object store but have no branch reference pointing to them.
- **Recovery via `git reflog` + `git cherry-pick`:** `git reflog` records all HEAD and branch-tip movements, including the branch deletion; search for the commit SHA immediately before the deletion event, then `git cherry-pick <sha>` onto the intended target branch. No need to recreate the deleted branch.
- **CRLF vs. LF on Windows `autocrlf`:** Windows Git defaults `core.autocrlf = true`, converting LF → CRLF on checkout and CRLF → LF on commit. Two files can therefore show as "different" in `git status`, shell `==` comparisons, or diff tools because one is CRLF in the working tree while the stored blob is LF — even though they are byte-for-byte identical inside Git.
- **Resolution for CRLF phantom diffs (`git update-index --refresh`):** CRLF-normalized files frequently show as phantom modified in `git status` after branch switches or IDE restarts. Running `git update-index --refresh` resets Git's internal index to match the current working-tree state under the active `autocrlf` policy, clearing false-positive "modified" flags without touching file content. Confirmed on 2026-06-17 to resolve accumulated CRLF index noise in FaceComps after a branch operation.
- **Worktree artifacts should be gitignored:** add `.claude/worktrees/` to `.gitignore` to prevent ephemeral worktree directories from appearing as untracked changes.
- **Windows MAX_PATH breaks worktree creation with deeply-nested long-filename dirs:** repos containing directories with deeply-nested files whose paths exceed 260 characters (e.g., a `SourcePapers/` folder with long PDF filenames) cause `git worktree add` and `EnterWorktree` to fail at the path-length limit. This failure is structural and unrelated to the content of the change being worked on.
- **Sparse-checkout workaround:** create the worktree with `--no-checkout`, then configure a sparse-checkout pattern that excludes the problematic directory (`SourcePapers/`) before checking out. This allows the worktree to be created and populated without ever materializing the long-path files on disk.
- **`.claude/settings.json` to disable background-isolation enforcement:** when worktree creation is structurally broken and sparse-checkout is impractical, adding `.claude/settings.json` with `{"backgroundIsolation": false}` to the repo prevents Claude Code from attempting worktree creation for background agents. The Write tool gate may block direct creation of this file; PowerShell shell mutations are not subject to the same guard and serve as a fallback.

## Details

The `ExitWorktree remove` behavior is easy to trigger accidentally because `remove` reads as a natural cleanup action after agent work in a worktree is done — the intent is "clean up the worktree," but the actual effect includes silently deleting the branch. If the agent made commits during the worktree session that were not merged or pushed, those commits become unreachable by branch name. Git's garbage collector typically does not collect unreachable objects for at least 30 days, so the commits are not immediately destroyed, but they are invisible to normal `git log` traversal and branch listings. The `git reflog` recovery path works because reflog records all reference updates including branch deletions: `git reflog | grep <branch-name>` (or a timestamp search) reveals the pre-deletion commit SHA, and `git cherry-pick` transfers those commits to the current branch without needing to recreate the deleted branch. Prevention: run `git status` and `git log` from inside the worktree before calling `ExitWorktree remove` to confirm all desired commits have been merged or pushed.

The CRLF/autocrlf normalization issue is a Windows-specific environment hazard that has nothing to do with actual file content — two files can fail a shell equality check (`==`) or appear as changed in `git status` while being semantically and functionally identical. This surfaces most sharply in repo-maintenance scripts that compare files byte-for-byte, such as the pre-commit hook described in [[concepts/model-agnostic-repo-dual-context-files]] that checks `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` for divergence. The diagnostic is to inspect raw bytes via `xxd`, PowerShell `Format-Hex`, or `cat -A` rather than trusting diff output or shell comparisons that operate on the working-tree representation. The most reliable cross-platform comparison for script use is `git hash-object <file>`, which hashes the stored blob (always LF after autocrlf normalization on commit) rather than the working-tree bytes. When phantom diffs accumulate after a branch switch or index-state mismatch, `git update-index --refresh` is the non-destructive resolution: it re-reads each tracked file's working-tree state, applies the current `autocrlf` policy to determine what the blob hash should be, and clears any "dirty" flags for files whose content has not actually changed relative to the last commit. On 2026-06-17, this command resolved CRLF index noise in the FaceComps repository after branch operations, with `git status` returning clean immediately afterward without any file modifications.

The Windows MAX_PATH limit failure is structurally different from the previous two gotchas because it is triggered by pre-existing repo content rather than by user actions during the worktree session. Repositories that contain legacy binary archives, PDF libraries (`SourcePapers/`), or deeply-nested generated output directories can accumulate file paths that exceed 260 characters. When `git worktree add` attempts to create a checkout in a new directory, it must materialize all tracked paths within the new worktree's root — any path that would exceed MAX_PATH causes the operation to fail. The sparse-checkout approach resolves this by instructing git to materialize only a subset of the tracked file tree, explicitly excluding the long-path directory from the worktree's scope. The change being made in the worktree (e.g., a UI component update in `src/`) does not require the `SourcePapers/` PDFs to be present, making sparse exclusion both safe and correct. If even sparse-checkout setup is too cumbersome for a given task, disabling background-isolation enforcement in `.claude/settings.json` prevents worktree creation altogether, reverting to inline execution on the main branch — appropriate when the change is demonstrably safe to make without isolation.

# Claude Code Three-Tier Memory Architecture

The Claude Code memory system is composed of three independent layers, each operating at a different granularity and owned by a different mechanism. This architecture was articulated on 2026-05-19 during a session that traced exactly when and how each capture mechanism fires. On 2026-06-05, a practical capacity-management routing pattern emerged for when Tier B global memory approaches its character cap. On 2026-06-18, a worked example clarified how to route a specific piece of context across the tiers — and which content should not enter the memory system at all.

## Key Points

- **Tier A — Native Claude Code auto-memory:** Built into Claude Code itself; managed per-project; no user configuration required. Operates automatically within a project context; its exact retention and synthesis mechanics are not user-visible.
- **Tier B — Custom global scratchpad via Stop hook:** A user-configured hook on the `Stop` event, which fires after every conversation turn. This provides incremental, per-turn transcript capture to a global scratchpad file (MEMORY.md) — a granularity that neither Tier A nor Tier C provides.
- **Tier C — claude-memory-compiler:** The [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] system: `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` hooks fire shell commands at session teardown or auto-compaction, spawning a detached `flush.py` process that appends structured notes to the daily log; at end-of-day these are compiled into knowledge articles.
- **The agent never sees a "session ending" event.** Session end and compaction are harness-level events; it is the Claude Code harness that runs the hook shell commands, not the agent itself.
- **PreCompact as a safety net:** In a long session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, preventing total context loss if the session later crashes before `SessionEnd`.
- **When Tier B is near cap, route to Tier A project files:** The global MEMORY.md (Tier B) has a character-cap constraint. When it approaches capacity, new durable facts should be saved to Tier A project-specific memory files (e.g., `project_<name>.md`, `user_career_timeline.md`), which are cross-project searchable via memsearch.
- **Content-to-tier routing matrix (2026-06-18):** file locations and versioning decisions belong in Tier B as an active-thread entry ("continue this next session"); durable personal conventions (e.g. "always save v1 before editing") belong in Tier A as a feedback rule; and the actual artifact content (slides, scripts) should NOT be duplicated in memory at all because it already lives on disk. Tier C's daily-log capture provides a compressed "what did I do that day" summary but is not a substitute for a durable artifact reference.

## Details

The three tiers are designed to capture context at different time horizons and granularities, and they operate independently rather than hierarchically. Tier A is fully opaque to the user. Tier B's Stop-hook scratchpad is the most granular: because the Stop event fires after every conversation turn, Tier B can capture mid-session context incrementally in near-real-time. Tier C produces the richest synthesized output — compiled knowledge articles from daily logs — but fires only at session boundaries.

The independence of the three tiers is their key reliability property. A failure in one does not cascade to the others: if a session crashes before `SessionEnd` fires, the Stop-hook's Tier B scratchpad may still contain the session's important turns. The "agent never sees session ending" detail is architecturally important: code written inside the agent context cannot detect or react to its own session ending. Teardown logic must be placed in hook shell commands that the harness executes.

The Tier B near-cap routing pattern (2026-06-05) addresses a practical capacity constraint. The correct response when Tier B is near capacity is not to compress existing entries — which risks discarding information encoded in current phrasing — but to route new durable facts into named Tier A project memory files, which are surfaced by memsearch across all project contexts.

The 2026-06-18 worked example makes the routing decision concrete and, importantly, identifies content that should stay out of memory entirely. Asked how best to preserve a working session's context (an RTP presentation's file locations, a v1/v2 versioning decision, and the slides/script themselves), the assistant produced a routing matrix rather than dumping everything into one tier: the file paths and versioning state map to Tier B because they describe an active thread to resume next session; a general preference like "always save v1 before editing" maps to Tier A as a durable feedback rule; and the actual slide and script content maps to neither — it already exists as files on disk, so copying it into memory would only create a stale duplicate. The distinction matters because the memory system's value is in cheap-to-retrieve pointers and rules, not in re-storing artifacts that a file path already addresses. The same example noted that Tier C's automatic daily-log capture is a lossy summary ("good for what did I do that day, not great for pick up exactly where I left off"), reinforcing that a deliberate Tier B pointer is the right tool when the goal is precise session continuity.
